segments.title: How castle engineering multiplies defensive power
segments.body: A castle turns available resources into a defensible structure through engineering and architecture. Its military advantage comes from allowing a small garrison to resist a much larger attacking force. The imbalance between defenders and attackers explains the value of castle construction. Fortification turns construction into a practical form of force multiplication.

evidence.note: Castles as large engineering and architectural works that allow a minimum number of defenders to resist a maximum number of attackers.

segments.summary: Castle engineering lets a small garrison defend against a much larger attacking force.

segments.title: Why medieval sea battles resembled land battles
segments.body: In this comparison, medieval sea battles are essentially land battles fought from ship to ship. The point is how closely combat ashore and afloat could resemble one another in the period. It also explains why land battles and naval warfare belong in the same discussion. The passage gives a concise link between the two settings.

evidence.note: An appreciative comparison of land and sea battles describes medieval naval combat as land battles fought from ship to ship.

segments.summary: Medieval sea battles could resemble land battles fought from ship to ship.
